match.reason: No point in the bank covers relative frequency as an estimate of probability from repeated trials; sample spaces covers theoretical probability from equally likely outcomes, which is a different idea.

draft.title: Relative frequency
card: A trial is one go at an experiment, such as one roll of a die. An event is an outcome you are counting, such as rolling a 6.
Relative frequency = number of times the event happened ÷ number of trials. It can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.
Example: Sam flips a drawing pin 50 times and it lands point up 30 times. Relative frequency = 30 ÷ 50 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%.
Relative frequency is used as an estimate of probability when the true value is not known. More trials usually give a better estimate.
draft.remember: Relative frequency = times it happened ÷ total trials, and more trials give a better estimate.

a.q: A spinner is spun 40 times and lands on red 14 times. What is the relative frequency of red?
a.why: Relative frequency = 14 ÷ 40 = 0.35. The tempting option 14/26 divides by the number of non-red spins, but the total number of trials must go on the bottom.
a.clue: Divide by the total number of spins.

b.q: Lena tests a coin she thinks is unfair. After 10 flips she gets 7 heads. Her friend Ravi flips the same coin 500 times and gets 270 heads. Which estimate of the probability of heads is likely to be better?
opts: Ravi's 270/500, because it uses more trials
Lena's 7/10, because it is a higher value
Lena's 7/10, because it is easier to write
Both are equally good, because it is one coin
b.why: More trials usually give a better estimate of probability, so Ravi's 270 ÷ 500 = 0.54 is likely closer to the true value. Lena's 7/10 = 0.7 comes from only a few flips, so chance can affect it a lot.
b.clue: Think about which result has more trials behind it.

b.best: Ravi's 270/500, because it uses more trials

problems.detail: The remember line says more trials 'give a better estimate' as a certainty, but the card correctly says more trials 'usually' give a better estimate. Put 'usually' back in so it matches the card.

The clue 'Think about which result has more trials behind it' matches the wording of the right option ('because it uses more trials'), so a student can pick it without understanding why more trials help.
